scope: D1507-F01 through D1507-F09 fixes in D1539 prose/0/text through prose/7/text and their directly affected saved paragraphs and adjacent section anchors. Not a redo of the immutable first review.
targetReader: Independent English reader aged 8-12 without algebra or geometry expertise.
summary: Eight findings are resolved. F07 is partially resolved: the original reference measurements are correctly separated, but cross-sectional area is still explained using the unexplained word area and the ambiguous phrase straight across. One short surface-versus-distance clarification is needed. The critical warning precedes the numerical pair; no printed mathematics, values, units, source objects, figures, captions, or tasks changed.

findingDispositions.assessment: Small total stretch now explicitly describes only this lesson's cast iron test piece. The adjacent steel sentence says it stretches much more, and the later approximately 15% value remains specimen-specific. Brittleness still means little plastic deformation, not universally small total strain.

Fracture and specimen have concrete first-use meanings; tension was already defined in prose/1. Plasticity includes lasting stretching, bending, squeezing, and other shape changes. Ductility is separately defined as permanent stretching before breaking in tension. Temperature, preparation, and loading qualifications remain.

Push/pull load and size/shape deformation precede elasticity. Recovery is explained before the conditions. Irreversible change, material state, and watching time have plain glosses. Approximate recovery, suitable temperature/loading, sufficiently small deformation, damage, irreversible change, stress, preparation, and time remain; small deformation alone is not a guarantee.

Strain is the added fraction of starting length; epsilon names it, and 1% means one added part per hundred original parts. Proportional is unpacked through doubling and linear through a straight-line graph before the rubber contrast. Recovery does not promise the doubling rule. The steel and rubber examples remain attributed and conditional.

Lasting plastic deformation is explicitly distinguished from being made of everyday plastic. Composition, loading speed, load duration, and time-dependent change are explained concretely. Wet clay, plastics, and lead are not fixed always-plastic categories.

A press is a machine that squeezes metal; hot working and forging by hammering/pressing are explained before their substantive use. Industrial-only framing, hot-deformation limits, and the non-universal lead temperature example remain. Neither example is an activity instruction.

The two engineering quantities are correctly separated and defined before the compact graph pair. Original gauge length is the starting measuring-point distance; engineering strain uses added length over that distance. Engineering stress uses original area, not necked current area. Necking, local true stress, and the force-per-square-metre unit are explained. The remaining barrier is that area straight across does not tell a geometry-novice child that area measures a whole flat surface rather than its width.

The explicit UNRECONCILED and NOT verified material constants warning and its plain-language explanation precede the first numerical pair. Numbers and curves are retained only for kinds of behavior, not reliable property calculation. The earlier Young's modulus example must not be combined with these data; verified stiffness, strength, and other material values are disallowed. Approximate endpoint and specimen-dependent/non-universal steel safeguards remain.

Stiffness has a resistance-to-change gloss. Steepness means a larger stress increase for the same small strain increase in the linear elastic range under comparable tensile tests. Brittleness is explicitly about little permanent deformation before breaking, not slope. Almost no remains approximate, and unresolved curves cannot supply reliable numerical slopes.

findings.title: Explain area as surface size, not distance across
findings.evidence: The original cross-sectional area is the area straight across a test piece before stretching.
findings.problem: This repeats area without explaining it. Straight across can mean the distance from one edge to the other, so a child without geometry knowledge can still confuse the engineering-stress denominator with width or diameter. The later measuring-point distance and square-metre unit do not resolve that distinction. This is the remaining part of F07's concrete-reference-measurement request, not a new source or pixel finding.
findings.smallestRepair: Replace only the first measurement sentence with a short surface-versus-distance explanation. Suggested wording: "The original cross-sectional area measures how much flat surface there is straight across the test piece before stretching. For a round test piece, picture the whole circle at its end, not just the distance across it." Keep the following engineering-stress definition unchanged.
findings.preserve: Original area before stretching; original measuring-point distance for engineering strain; current local area only for local true stress; all existing math, values, units, warnings, source metadata, figures, and captions.
findings.qualification: The round test piece is a conditional explanatory picture, not a claim that the printed historical specimens had a newly verified shape or a prompt to calculate circle area.
findings.affectedFlowRepair: Update the corresponding saved paragraph text. No section boundary refers to this paragraph, so the three boundary pairs need no change for this repair.
